South Florida enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with a 25-8 overall record and a 15-3 American Athletic Conference record, finishing as the AAC regular-season champion and No. 1 seed in the league tournament. USF’s team statistical profile is unusually clear: the Bulls score 87.7 points per game, allow 75.5, average 42.7 rebounds, 17.2 assists, 9.2 steals, and force 14.3 opponent turnovers per game while committing only 11.2 themselves. That combination of pace, offensive freedom, glass work, and turnover pressure is the foundation of this team. USF also produced 19.1 points off turnovers per game and attempted 958 threes in 33 games, a strong numerical indicator that Bryan Hodgson’s offense is built around drive-and-kick creation, early-clock threes, and transition attack rather than pure half-court post-up basketball. ([gousfbulls.com](https://gousfbulls.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Offensively, South Florida plays like a modern spread attack with old-school rebounding force behind it. The specific tendencies show up in both team totals and game patterns. USF made 318 threes in 33 games, or 9.6 per game, while also getting to the line 894 times, or 27.1 free-throw attempts per game. That is a high-volume blend of perimeter spacing and downhill pressure. In practice, that means CJ Brown initiates, Wes Enis and Joseph Pinion stretch the floor, and Izaiyah Nelson punishes rotations as a rim finisher and offensive rebounder. In the January 22 road win at UAB, Pinion hit six threes and scored 25 points while Nelson posted 16 points and 10 rebounds, a textbook example of USF’s inside-out structure. In the March 8 win over Charlotte, Pinion scored 22 with four threes while Enis added 20 points, seven rebounds, and six assists, showing that when opponents overplay the first action, Enis can become a secondary playmaker. Against Memphis on March 5, Enis scored 29 on 9-of-17 shooting and 9-of-9 at the line, while Josh Omojafo added 21 on 7-of-9 shooting and 3-of-4 from three; that balance suggests USF can flow from ball-screen attack into weak-side kickouts and slot threes without becoming one-dimensional. ([gousfbulls.com](https://gousfbulls.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

The named personnel defines the scheme. Enis is the volume movement-and-pull-up shooter at 16.8 points per game with 107 made threes and a .365 three-point percentage. Pinion is the second elite spacer at 14.2 points per game with 106 made threes at .379. Brown is the lead organizer at 11.1 points and 4.8 assists per game, and his 158 assists are the best raw playmaking number on the roster. Nelson is the interior hub: 15.7 points, 9.6 rebounds, 54 steals, and 45 blocks while shooting .562 from the field. Omojafo gives them a physical slasher/finisher at 11.5 points and 5.3 rebounds. A useful lineup tell: USF had two players reach 100 made threes by March 8, Enis and Pinion, which is why opponents are constantly forced into long closeouts that open driving lanes and weak-side rebounding chances for Nelson and Omojafo. ([gousfbulls.com](https://gousfbulls.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Defensively, the philosophy is pressure first, disruption second, and cleanup by Nelson on the back line. The raw numbers are strong: 303 steals in 33 games, 9.2 per game, and a +3.1 turnover margin. USF also held opponents to .413 shooting overall. They are not a pure shutdown three-point defense, allowing opponents .339 from deep, so the scheme is better described as aggressive at the point of attack than conservative on the arc. A specific in-game example came in the January 31 loss at Temple. USF’s own recap noted that the Bulls shifted into zone around the 8:45 mark of the first half to disrupt Temple’s rhythm, and the change limited dribble penetration and ball movement. That matters for tournament scouting because it shows Hodgson’s staff is willing to toggle coverages within games rather than sit in one base shell. Another example came in the February 25 win at Rice: USF held Rice to 14 points by the 5:45 mark of the second half, and the recap specifically tied that stretch to stops turning into transition scoring. Against Wichita State on February 11, South Florida erased a seven-point halftime deficit and held the Shockers to 28 second-half points in a 66-58 road win, which is a strong marker for halftime defensive adjustment. ([gousfbulls.com](https://gousfbulls.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Bryan Hodgson’s coaching philosophy shows up as tempo, spacing, and aggressive correction during games. His background matters here: USF hired him on March 24, 2025 after two successful seasons at Arkansas State, where he led back-to-back 20-win seasons and a 25-win 2024-25 campaign. At USF, his first season immediately produced AAC Coach of the Year honors, while Nelson was named AAC Player of the Year, Defensive Player of the Year, and Newcomer of the Year. The adjustment history is documented by game. In the January 18 overtime loss to Wichita State, USF trailed 30-15 in the first half but answered with an 8-0 run, then a larger 33-8 surge bridging halftime to take control, evidence that the staff can identify pressure points and flip momentum with tactical changes. In the January 31 Temple game, the move to zone altered the game flow. In the February 11 Wichita State road win, USF again changed the texture after halftime and dominated the second half. Traditional analysts care about whether a coach can win the second game within the game; Hodgson’s first season says yes. ([gousfbulls.com](https://gousfbulls.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/coaches/bryan-hodgson/5284?utm_source=openai))

Late-game and clutch execution is real but not flawless. The best positive example is January 22 at UAB, when USF closed a statement 82-69 road win behind Pinion’s 25 points and Nelson’s 16-and-10. Another is March 5 at Memphis, a 96-89 win in which USF handled a hostile road environment and got 29 from Enis; the box score shows Isaiah Jones hit a free throw with 19 seconds left to push the lead to five, a specific late-game closeout possession. March 1 against Tulane was not technically clutch because USF won 90-62, but it mattered under title pressure and the Bulls responded with a no-drama blowout. On the negative side, January 31 at Temple is the cautionary example: Nelson’s dunk gave USF a 78-77 lead with 22 seconds left, but Temple answered and USF lost 79-78. January 18 versus Wichita State is another warning sign: USF erased a 15-point deficit, forced overtime, and still lost 86-85. So the profile is this: USF can execute late, but in true coin-flip endings they have shown some vulnerability. ([gousfbulls.com](https://gousfbulls.com/news/2026/1/23/mens-basketball-usf-mens-basketball-earns-82-69-statement-win-over-uab.aspx?utm_source=openai))

The key players all have defined tournament roles. Enis is the headliner shot-maker. He averages 16.8 points and had a 36-point game with a program-record 10 made threes against UAB on January 4, even though USF lost 109-106 in double overtime. That game is the clearest evidence that he can create offense against high pressure in big-possession games. Nelson is the anchor on both ends at 15.7 points and 9.6 rebounds; he posted 24 points and 8 rebounds at Rice on February 25, then followed with 14 points, 13 rebounds, and a career-high six assists against Tulane on March 1. Pinion is the swing shooter at 14.2 points per game; his 25 points with six threes at UAB on January 22 and 22 points versus Charlotte on March 8 are high-value proof that he can tilt games with spacing. Brown is the control guard; his 4.8 assists per game and 158 total assists make him the player who keeps the ball moving to the right shot. Omojafo is the quiet pressure point: his 21 points against Memphis on March 5 gave USF a needed second slasher when Pinion struggled. ([gousfbulls.com](https://gousfbulls.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

The notable wins tell you why South Florida is dangerous. January 7 at North Texas, 74-70, showed road toughness after a 25-30 halftime deficit. January 22 at UAB, 82-69, ended a seven-game losing streak in the series and showed that USF could beat an athletic league rival away from home. January 25 against Florida Atlantic, 89-75, was a second-half separation win in front of 4,833 fans and confirmed that the Bulls’ offense could overwhelm a quality opponent. February 11 at Wichita State, 66-58, was the first-place swing game; USF erased a halftime deficit and took sole possession of the league lead. March 5 at Memphis, 96-89, was the loudest win on the résumé because it came with the regular-season title race still live and required offensive poise in the final minute. The losses are also revealing. The January 4 109-106 double-overtime loss to UAB showed defensive limitations in extended games. The January 18 86-85 overtime loss to Wichita State showed that even after a huge comeback, USF can struggle to finish. The January 31 79-78 loss at Temple exposed end-of-game fragility. The December 17 loss at Alabama, 104-93, showed they can score against top-level athletes but also give up too much in transition and secondary break. ([gousfbulls.com](https://gousfbulls.com/sports/mens-basketball/opponent-history/university-of-north-texas/302?utm_source=openai))

As for Hodgson’s NCAA tournament history as a head coach, this is his first NCAA Tournament appearance. His USF coach bio identifies South Florida’s March 24, 2025 hire as his first season in Tampa after two seasons as Arkansas State’s head coach, and the available official biography credits him with back-to-back 20-win seasons and a postseason appearance there, but not a previous NCAA Tournament berth as a head coach. So for tournament-history purposes, 2026 is his first trip leading a team into the bracket. ([gousfbulls.com](https://gousfbulls.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/coaches/bryan-hodgson/5284?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: South Florida is a veteran, pressure-oriented, rebound-winning team whose ceiling is driven by three things that travel in March: Enis and Pinion making threes, Nelson controlling the paint, and the defense generating steals that become runout points. The concern is equally specific: when the game slows into a final-minute possession battle, the Bulls have multiple one-possession losses on the record. That makes USF a dangerous but volatile NCAA Tournament team, exactly the type of high-variance conference champion that can both spring an upset and get dragged into a nerve game.

South Florida enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a very specific kind of problem: a pace-and-pressure offense built to turn games into possession races. Through the regular season, Bryan Hodgson’s first USF team was 23-8, won the American regular-season title, averaged 88.4 points per game, and posted a 117.9 offensive rating. USF’s own game notes listed the Bulls at 88.2 points per game entering March 1, first in the American in assists (17.0), free throws made (20.8), free throw attempts (28.0), and three-point attempts (29.1), while USF Athletics described the Memphis matchup as being played at the league’s “conference-leading pace.” That combination tells you exactly what they want: early offense, paint pressure, rim runs, kick-out threes, and enough tempo to magnify their depth and foul-drawing. To beat them, you cannot let the game become an up-and-down whistle game. You must make them execute late in the clock, win the defensive glass, and force them to score against a set half-court shell. Example: when Alabama beat USF 104-93 on December 17, even a strong USF scoring night was not enough because the game became too efficient on both sides; against VCU, USF was held to 66 in a much more disruptive game. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/south-florida/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

The most reliable tactical way to disrupt USF’s style is to attack the sources of its efficiency rather than the raw scoring total. USF gets a huge share of offense from free throws, second shots, and transition-triggering turnovers. In mid-December, USF ranked No. 2 nationally in free throws made per game at 21.9, No. 4 in attempts at 29.5, No. 6 in offensive rebounds at 15.5 per game, and No. 20 in turnovers forced at 16.4 per game with a +4.6 turnover margin. That means the anti-USF recipe is concrete: stay down on shot fakes, switch with physicality on the wing to prevent straight-line drives, send two bodies to Nelson and Collins on the glass, and prioritize ball security over tempo. If you give them live-ball turnovers, the game gets away from you fast. Early-season evidence is clear: USF forced 21 turnovers from both Florida A&M and George Washington, 18 from Coppin State, and 14 from Kennesaw State in its first four tracked examples, while also recording 13 steals against FAMU, GW, and Oklahoma State. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/documents/download/2025/12/16/USF_MBB_Game_11_vs._Alabama.pdf))

On press vulnerability: the available 2026 public sources do not provide a clean possession-level “vs press” table for USF, so the best evidence is turnover response in named games. The strongest red flag is the January 31 loss at Temple, where USF’s pregame notes for the next game referenced Temple forcing a USF season-high 18 turnovers. A second warning sign came in the overtime home loss to Wichita State, a game USF lost 86-85 despite its normal scoring environment; that is the kind of game where the opponent kept USF from cleanly controlling tempo. In contrast, when USF handled pressure and played through it, the Bulls still exploded: 97-83 at Tulane, 89-75 over FAU, and 96-89 at Memphis. So the scouting conclusion is specific: USF is not inherently fragile with the ball, but aggressive guard pressure can push them above their normal 11.5-11.6 turnovers per game and drag them away from their preferred flow. Make CJ Brown and Wes Enis play east-west before they play north-south. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/usf.sidearmsports.com/documents/2026/2/13/USF_MBB_Game_26_at_FAU.pdf))

On zone vulnerability: the public sources do not expose a formal “zone efficiency” split, so the right inference has to come from shot profile and game outcomes. USF is a high-volume but only moderate-efficiency three-point shooting team: .331 from three entering the FAU game, .337 entering the Temple game, and .331 entering the Tulane game, despite ranking first in the AAC in three-point attempts. That is important. A team that shoots many threes but makes them at roughly 33% can be coaxed into lower-value offense if a zone removes paint catches and offensive rebounding angles. VCU’s 78-66 win is the clearest low-output data point against a disciplined defensive opponent, and Alabama’s win is the clearest example that simply playing fast is not enough. The actionable takeaway: a compact 2-3 or matchup zone can work only if it finishes possessions with rebounding; if your back line does not hit first, Nelson, Collins, and Jones can turn zone possessions into foul shots and putbacks. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/usf.sidearmsports.com/documents/2026/2/13/USF_MBB_Game_26_at_FAU.pdf))

USF’s preferred pace is fast, and forcing the opposite is mandatory. Personnel-wise, USF is big on the wing and long in the frontcourt, but not overwhelming at lead guard. The likely guard line is CJ Brown (6-2, 175), Wes Enis (6-2, 200), and Joseph Pinion/Josh Omojafo/Devin Haid on the wings at 6-5. Third, use selective zone or a packed-gap man-to-man to bait USF’s volume three-point habit; they attempt a lot of threes, but their team percentage sat around 33%. Fourth, send at least two defenders back on every shot to kill early offense and make Brown initiate in the half court. Fifth, finish possessions with gang rebounding, because USF was still averaging 42.9 rebounds per game entering March and had a 21-offensive-rebound game against FAU. If you fail on any two of those five, they can get to 85+ quickly. If you force half-court possessions, keep them off the line, and win the first-shot rebound battle, they become much more beatable than their raw scoring average suggests.
